sections.title: What the partnership is.
cols: Annual training — your engineers trained every year on the platform and every module, on the six manuals and the flight-test documents, and on what shipped since the last session.
Unlimited technical support — every implementation you sign has our support behind it, without a ticket quota. You honour your projects; we make sure you can.
A technological edge — where your market needs a driver, a protocol variant or a functionality to win a challenging project, we build it. That is how you take the projects others cannot.
The services are yours — engineering, installation, training and support at the client: entirely your revenue.

Not a nicer SCADA — what you sell is not a nicer SCADA. It is the complete execution system and the complete maintenance system, on the SCADA's own database, on the PLCs your client already has — installed from scripts in a single session.

sections.title: The SCADA, live to the phone
sections.alt: an engineer and an apprentice at a line panel, a hand on the touch screen

sections.title: Live, from the wall panel to the phone.
cols: Purely web — the same live pages follow a user from the control room to a phone, with nothing installed and nothing licensed per screen. A panel can be pinned to one line in kiosk mode.
Three languages, one design — three languages, right-to-left Arabic included, from one design.

Pages — synoptics drawn once, served everywhere. Tap any pump or motor for its faceplate: live values, a raw mini-trend, its journal alarms, its commands. Equipment symbols that carry their own maintenance knowledge.
Alarms — prioritised, acknowledged, shelved with a reason. A flood is named with its rate, its target and the area behind it. An audit-grade journal that survives a tag delete or a redesign.
Commands — every command attributed and timestamped, refused in the database when the user may not, and switched off during replay.
Access — row-level security in the database, not a hidden menu in the client. What a user may not see never reaches a screen, an export or a sheet.

The whole platform, in the operator's hand — not a viewer app beside the product: the same three applications, sized for a hand. The operator's HMI, the engineer's editor and the administrator's console all open on a phone with nothing installed, the same rights, the same live data, the same three languages.
The technician's tool — take the job, work the frozen checklist with each reading judged at the box, take the spare from the shelf, add a photograph, sign the close.
The alarm insights are the ones ISA-18.2 and EEMUA 191 ask for — the rate against its target, the response times, the flood episodes.

sections.title: TimeLens and Tag Lens
sections.alt: a service desk at night, two screens and a lamp, an engineer from behind

sections.title: Two lenses: one over time, one over the tags.
cols: The operator's question is "what happened at 16:03?". The engineer's question is "where is this tag used, and what breaks if I change it?". Each has a lens, and each answers from the one database.
The historian is part of the platform, not a product beside it. TimeLens replays any synoptic from it like a recorder — with no second recorder to buy.

Read the plant like an instrument — lanes or overlay, live or any window. Cursors that read minimum, average, maximum and delta over the span. Annotations that survive a reload. An alarm lane over the pens.
Share what you found — CSV and PNG in one press, and a link that opens the same view for a colleague.
Rewind any screen — back and forward at half to sixty times speed, alarm to alarm, to a moment, with a link to that moment you can paste.
The gold dress — the replayed screen wears gold so it can never be mistaken for live, and commands are off.
From an alarm to the screen — from an alarm row, one press lands on the screen as it was when the alarm fired.
Numbers that survive an audit — averages are count-weighted, never an average of averages. A quality byte rides every reading. The right tier of history serves every zoom.
A correction reaches every total — correct a value from years ago and every total since corrects itself.
The thread — every page, trend, alarm, report block, formula and condition that uses one tag, counted live from the database, never from a stale report.
The what-if painter — rename, re-address or delete, and every dependent card shows its own fate before you touch anything.
The health sweep — orphans polled and shown nowhere, ghost bindings, formulas that no longer parse.
Why an integrator cares — a migration is a thousand tags moved. The Tag Lens shows what each one touches before you move it, and the health sweep shows what you left behind.
We know of no other platform that follows one tag through every module of the plant like this.

sections.title: The editor and the engine
sections.alt: the rack dark and the line still running, an operator at a steel-built panel

sections.title: Engineered in a browser. Served from the edge.
cols: Nothing installed, nothing licensed per workstation. Several engineers on the same page at once, a live preview against the running line, and a whole line that travels as one file to the next plant.
Presence, not a lock — a presence banner that never blocks; a stale save refused rather than silently merged; every page, symbol and trend versioned.
Duplicate, export, import — a line is duplicated in one press, exported as one portable file, and imported on the next plant with every binding intact.
Symbols that know the machine — a curated library of equipment symbols by family, each drawn to the process scale and each carrying the failure vocabulary the maintenance module picks from.
Draw the pump once; the maintenance record already knows what a pump breaks.
One program at the edge — beside the PLC it polls, evaluates, buffers and serves, and runs redundant against the same devices.
The protocols — SOP supports all major drivers, Modbus, OPC DA, Siemens S7 and OPC UA among them.
The centre only receives — the edge polls, evaluates and serves, so a dead server loses no plant data.
The emergency HMI — when the server is unreachable, the edge serves the plant's real pages on the plant network until it is back.
Three substrates, one install — installs from scripts in a single session: on-prem, air-gapped, or on a cloud backbone.
The engineer's editor, on the floor — the page tree, the tags, the equipment, the Tag Lens and a line's readiness, from the plant floor, beside the machine being commissioned.
The administrator's console — the fleet of edges with their last beat, enrollments waiting for approval, users and grants, the health of the backend and the historian, the audit journal.

sections.title: EMS, CMMS and EPS, with the SCADA
sections.alt: the end of a packaging line, cases on the rollers, a tablet with the day's schedule

sections.title: The complete EMS and CMMS, integrated with the SCADA.
cols: In the class, the execution system, the maintenance system and the report server are separate products with their own databases and licences, joined by an integration project. Here they are the same rows. That is the whole difference, and it is the one your client can price.

EMS · execution — plant model, materials and stock, products, recipes behind a quality door, orders on a calendar. Jobs the line starts and ends itself; batches that overlap like lines do; a batch record where every number says who measured it.

CMMS · no data entry — the machine's type plants parts, plans, checklists and failure words. Meters folded from the run record; the fault turned into a job in one tap; the technician on a phone; a parts ledger; a signed close that seals the record.

EPS · performance — the run signal and the counters fold once, on the server. The operator is asked once, at the restart, in two taps. Losses priced in time, units and money; two honest OEEs; the page printed as paper in one press.
Integrated by birth — a released maintenance job books a planned window the performance engine already honours. The batch certificate prints from the engine that prints the shift handover.
The lab outranks the counter — a reject count signed by the lab outranks the counter, and the period says it was restated.
One security model reaches the report.
Nothing to connect, because there is nothing to connect.

sections.title: A reporting engine, not a report server
sections.alt: a standing desk at the edge of the hall, the shift handover signed on paper

sections.title: A reporting engine, not a report server.
cols: What the incumbents sell as a separate report server with its own designer, its own database and its own licence is an organ of SOP. Design a report once against real tags; the platform computes it, seals it, signs it and delivers it, with nobody watching.
01 Design — blocks bound to real tags: tiles with targets, period tables, trends with their limits, alarm journals, consumption and cost, the performance cascade, the maintenance blocks.
02 Compute — on the server, in the site's own clock: every shift, day, week or month, every batch or order, every maintenance job, or when a plant condition fires. Nobody presses anything.
03 Seal — frozen on arrival, numbered, hashed. Run it again and you get a second document beside the first, never a refresh.
04 Sign — by name and capacity, proved with the signer's own password, bound to the hash, never edited and never withdrawn.
05 Deliver — printed on the plant's letterhead in three languages, e-mailed to the list, filed as a PDF, exported.
Zero report servers — the engine runs on the backend already installed. A small worker beside it files the PDF and posts it to the list.
Zero third-party licences — no reporting product, no rendering licence, no designer bought separately. It is inside the platform.
Zero seats to read — every operator, supervisor, planner and auditor reads, prints, exports and signs.
The sheets a plant runs on — the shift handover, the batch certificate, the maintenance record, the audit sheet for critical equipment, the excursion report, the monthly review.
A blank certificate is refused while it is being designed.

Read it before you buy it — six manuals cover every screen of every module; a flight-test document per module tells a tester how to exercise the whole feature on a real rig, start to finish.
The estate — SOP is already running on several production lines.
